sections.title: Lesson 03: Transformer accounting and speculative inference

keyTerms.definition: Unit 03 of CS229S, covering transformer accounting and speculative inference.
The evidence label on every lesson claim, here PLANNED with source attribution pending.

recall.question: What unit and concepts does this lesson cover?
recall.answer: Unit cs229s-U03, concepts C01 to C12, calendar-anchored to Week 2, Oct 04, Analyzing the Performance of Transformers.

keyTerms.definition: The fixed structure every concept carries, from source and scope to visual units.
The shared symbols file this lesson follows.

recall.question: What source does speculative decoding follow here?
recall.answer: Leviathan et al. and Chen et al. (2023), taught from the papers.

keyTerms.definition: Full training FLOP count: dense term plus the attention term.
12 L n T D: the quadratic-in-T part of the training FLOP count.
The dense-only estimate that undercounts by 2.3x at T = 32768.

recall.question: Write the full training FLOP formula.
recall.answer: C = 6PD + 12 L n T D.

recall.question: For P = 7e9, D = 1e12, L = 32, n = 4096, T = 2048, what are the two terms?
recall.answer: 6PD = 4.2e22, attention = 3.2e21, total about 4.5e22. Attention is about 7 percent.

recall.question: At what context length does the attention term exceed the dense term?
recall.answer: Past T ~ 6n. At T = 32768, n = 4096, the attention term is 1.33x the dense term.

keyTerms.definition: FLOPs per decode token for the weights: one multiply-add per parameter.
The stored keys and values that remove recompute during decode.
Limited by bytes moved, not FLOPs: decode at batch 1.

recall.question: Write the per-token decode FLOP formula.
recall.answer: 2P + 4LTn per token.

recall.question: P = 13e9, 50 tokens. Decode FLOPs?
Two models have the same FLOPs but one decodes 3x faster. Explain.
recall.answer: The faster one moves fewer bytes: e.g. int8 weights, same 2P FLOPs, 4x less traffic. Count bytes.

keyTerms.definition: Per token per layer: 2n numbers (key + value). Total: 2BTLn numbers.
The cache memory scaling in batch, tokens, layers, and width.
Finer cache allocation that reduces fragmentation waste.

recall.question: Write the KV byte formula.
recall.answer: Bytes = 2 * B * T * L * n * bytes-per-element, i.e. 4BTLn in fp16.

recall.question: Serving OOMs only on long requests. Name the term and a fix.
recall.answer: The KV cache: at B = 8, T = 8192 it is 34 GB, bigger than the 14 GB weights. Fix: size the cache first, or use paged attention.

keyTerms.definition: The prompt-processing phase: forward pass on all prompt tokens at once.
Dominated by prefill at long prompts.
Splitting the prompt into pieces when its score matrix exceeds memory.

recall.question: Define prefill in one line.
recall.answer: Prefill reads all prompt tokens at once (parallel, like training) and builds the KV cache for the prompt.

recall.question: P = 7e9, T = 8192. Prefill FLOPs, dense term only?
First token takes 10 s at T = 65536. Name the term.
recall.answer: The quadratic attention scores: naive (128K)^2 scores can hit 32 GB per head-set. Chunk or tile.

keyTerms.definition: FLOPs per byte moved: prefill ~T, decode ~1 at batch 1 (fp16).
About T FLOP/byte: weights are reused across T tokens.
About 1 FLOP/byte at batch 1: each weight is used once.

recall.question: Write both intensities.
recall.answer: Prefill: I ~ T FLOP/byte. Decode: I ~ B FLOP/byte (about 1 at batch 1, fp16).

recall.question: Toy ridge 150. Classify prefill T = 64 and decode B = 200.
recall.answer: Prefill I ~ 64 < 150: memory-bound. Decode I ~ 200 > 150: compute-bound.

recall.question: Decode got no faster with 2x bandwidth. Explain.
recall.answer: At large batch decode turns compute-bound (e.g. B = 512 gives I ~ 512 > 150), so adding bandwidth does nothing.

keyTerms.definition: Serving many requests together to share the weight read.
Tokens/s across the batch: rises sublinearly with B, then flattens.
Seconds per token for one request: rises with B.

recall.question: Define the batching tradeoff in one line.
recall.answer: The bus versus the taxi: batching carries many at lower cost each, but everyone waits for boarding.

recall.question: Batch 1: 20 ms/token. With the toy model, batch 16 latency and total throughput?
Batch 32 throughput is flat vs batch 16 but latency doubled. Diagnose.
recall.answer: Past the compute roof: batching adds latency with no throughput gain. Find the knee (C05).

keyTerms.definition: A small fast model q that proposes gamma tokens per round.
Draft length: tokens proposed per speculative round.
a: per-token probability the target keeps a draft token.

recall.question: Define c, gamma, a in one line each.
recall.answer: c = t_draft / t_target per token, cost ratio. gamma = tokens proposed per round. a = per-token acceptance probability.

recall.question: c = 0.05, gamma = 5, a = 0.8. E[k] and speedup?
recall.answer: E[k] = 3.689. Cost per round 1.25. Per token 0.34 target-steps. Speedup about 2.95x.

recall.question: Speedup < 1. Name two causes with the numbers to check.
recall.answer: Slow draft (c ~ 0.5) or low acceptance (a ~ 0.3): c = 0.5, gamma = 5, a = 0.3 gives 2.46x slower than baseline. Measure a and c first.

keyTerms.definition: The target's one parallel pass over the gamma draft tokens.
The extra distribution the target computes after the last draft token.

recall.question: Why is verification one step, not gamma?
recall.answer: Grading a quiz versus taking it: the drafts are known tokens, so the target computes all gamma+1 distributions in parallel, like a prefill.

recall.question: gamma = 8, slope 0.05. Verification steps?
Verification takes 4 steps at gamma = 5. Name the cause.
recall.answer: At large gamma the pass becomes compute-heavy and exceeds 1 step. Model it as 1 + slope*gamma.

keyTerms.definition: The acceptance rule that makes speculative output exactly p-distributed.
The mental model: the target admits a draft token with probability min(1, p/q).
min(1, p(x_i)/q(x_i)) per draft token.

recall.question: Write the accept probability.
recall.answer: Accept x_i with probability min(1, p(x_i)/q(x_i)).

recall.question: q(cat) = 0.7, p(cat) = 0.2. Accept prob?
recall.answer: 0.2/0.7 = 0.286. On reject, resample from the positive part of (p - q).

recall.question: q = p exactly. What is a?
recall.answer: a = 1: every draft accepts.

keyTerms.definition: The output distribution is exactly p, not approximately: a photocopy, not a sketch.
A1: draft and target share the vocabulary and tokenization.
The mental model: rejection sampling is a mathematical identity.

recall.question: Name the two exactness assumptions.
recall.answer: A1: draft and target share the vocabulary and tokenization. A2: the resample distribution is norm(max(0, p-q)), computed exactly.

recall.question: Outputs look off after a tokenizer change. Explain.
recall.answer: Mismatched tokenizers put the distributions over different spaces and the proof breaks. Same tokenizer is mandatory.

recall.question: Resample skipped on reject (just drop). Is output still p?
recall.answer: No: the residual mass max(0, p - q) must be covered by the resample for the total to equal p.

keyTerms.definition: alpha: per-token probability the target keeps a draft token.
Expected tokens per round: (1 - a^{gamma+1}) / (1 - a).
The mental model: each draft token is a free throw with make probability a.

recall.question: Write the E[k] formula.
a = 0.6, gamma = 4. E[k]?
Formula says 3.7, measured 2.1. Explain.
recall.answer: Constant a is a simplification: real acceptance falls with position (later drafts condition on earlier drafts). Fit per-position a_i.

keyTerms.definition: E[k] = gamma*c + 1: the point where speculative decoding pays.
E[k] / (gamma*c + 1).

recall.question: Write the speedup formula.
recall.answer: Speedup = E[k] / (gamma*c + 1).

recall.question: a = 0.9, gamma = 7, c = 0.1. Speedup?
Measured 1.2x, formula 2.9x. Name two causes.
recall.answer: Verification slope larger than modeled, or acceptance rate lower on the real workload. Measure a and the verification slope.

keyTerms.definition: The unit's bottom line: count the bytes per token, then buy back latency.
Cached decode, batched prefill, speculative rounds.

recall.question: What does the unit chapter plate contrast?
recall.answer: Naive serving (recompute, no batching, serial verify) vs the managed system (cached decode, batched prefill, speculative rounds). Bottom line: count the bytes per token, then buy back latency.

keyTerms.definition: The Shell 0 observable: more than one token per target step without changing the distribution.
Accept with min(1, p/q), resample from norm(max(0, p-q)).

recall.question: What is the Shell 3 rule of the speculative-decoding ladder?
recall.answer: Accept with min(1, p/q), resample from norm(max(0, p-q)).

recall.question: What breaks exactness (Shell 7)?
recall.answer: Breaking the same-tokenizer assumption: exactness fails.

keyTerms.definition: The speedup formula and its break-even, checked before any speculative serving work.
C05: designs the serving stack for the LLM engineer.

recall.question: What is the research engineer's pre-flight check before speculative serving?
recall.answer: The speedup formula and its break-even.
